content.text:
Create an animated, non-interactive surfing pelican using html/3js

Build this as an interactive web page in the current directory.
- The entry point is index.html. Put your code in JavaScript ES modules loaded from it
  (`<script type="module" src="main.js">`), and add a short README.md.
- You may use npm packages: `npm install <package>` here, then import them by name
  (`import * as THREE from "three"`). No CDN URLs and no import maps.
- Afterwards the page is packaged into one self-contained index.html with esbuild: every script and
  stylesheet index.html references is bundled with everything it imports. Load assets the page needs
  with `import` (they become data URLs) or generate them in code, never by URL string.
- The packaged page runs offline in a sandboxed iframe: no network requests, and no localStorage,
  cookies or other storage (they throw there).
- Check that it packages: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` must succeed.
  Don't build or package the page yourself; that happens afterwards.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you built.

# Surfing Pelican

A non-interactive three.js animation: a brown pelican rides the barrel of a
breaking wave at sunset, wings out for balance.

Open `index.html` through any bundler or dev server that resolves bare imports
(for example `npx esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --servedir=. --outdir=.
--serve`). The only dependency is `three`. Everything else, including textures,
is generated in code, so the page needs no network access and no storage.

## What's on screen

- **Breaking wave** (`src/wave.js`, `src/ocean.js`): one continuous ocean mesh.
  Near the break, its rows follow a Catmull-Rom wave profile that morphs along the
  line from an unbroken shoulder, through the pocket and a full overhanging tube,
  into collapsing whitewater. The scene sits in the frame that travels with the
  surfer, so the wave holds still while the water, foam and chop stream past.
  The shader handles ripple normals, Fresnel sky reflection, light glowing
  through the thin lip, the wave hiding the sky in reflections of the water in
  front of it, procedural foam (lip, whitewater, marbled face lines, scum lines)
  and haze towards the horizon.
- **Pelican** (`src/pelican.js`): lofted body, neck and bill with a sagging gular
  pouch. Wings are bone chains covered in about 60 individual feathers each. The
  pelican balances with its wings, flaps now and then, keeps its head steady in
  world space, glances back at the tube, blinks, and its pouch jiggles. Its legs
  use two-bone IK down to webbed feet planted on the board.
- **Surfing** (`src/surfer.js`): the board follows the wave face, carves up and
  down, and banks into turns. The pelican leans out with the board whenever the
  tube wall gets close to its head.
- **Effects** (`src/spray.js`, `src/trail.js`): rail spray, mist blown off the
  crest by the offshore wind, drops falling from the lip, whitewater bursts, and
  a foamy carve line.
- **Sky** (`src/sky.js`, `src/shaders.js`): a procedural sunset with clouds. The
  same function lights the scene via PMREM and feeds the water's reflections.
  There is also a hazy headland, and a line of pelicans gliding past
  (`src/flock.js`).
- **Camera** (`src/camera.js`): a loop of four shots (front three-quarter, down
  the line into the tube, low and close, wide) with slow glides between them.

Post-processing is bloom, ACES tone mapping and a light vignette. The render
resolution adapts automatically to keep the frame rate smooth.

I built the surfing pelican scene in three.js. The required check `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` passes; the only output is esbuild's normal note that the bundle is 1.3 MB, which is mostly three.js. I checked the look by rendering frames in headless Chrome throughout the camera loop, in landscape and portrait.

**What's in the scene**
- **The wave:** a breaking wave at sunset with a curl that overhangs into a full tube. Along its length it goes from smooth unbroken water ahead of the pelican, through the tube, to whitewater behind. The scene moves with the pelican, so the wave holds still while foam and ripples stream past to show speed.
- **Water look:** the thin lip glows when backlit, and foam forms on the lip edge, as thin lines on the face and as lacy patches in front. The water in front of the wave reflects the wave rather than open sky.
- **The pelican:** a brown pelican with a long hooked bill, a dark pouch that jiggles, eye rings and webbed feet. Each wing has about 66 separate feathers. It keeps its wings spread for balance and flaps now and then. Its head stays steady while the body moves, it looks back at the tube from time to time, and it blinks.
- **Surfing:** the board carves up and down the face and leans into turns, and the legs bend to keep the feet planted on the deck. If the tube wall gets too close to the pelican's head, it leans out with the board. I added this after finding its head had disappeared inside the wave.
- **Extras:** spray off the board, mist blown off the crest, drops falling from the lip, whitewater bursts, and a foam trail behind the board. There's also a sunset sky with clouds that lights the scene, a hazy headland, and a line of pelicans gliding past in the distance.
- **Camera:** it loops through four shots with slow glides between them: front three-quarter, looking down the wave into the tube, low and close, and a wide view.

The picture gets bloom, tone mapping and a light vignette. Render resolution drops automatically if the frame rate falls. Every texture is generated in code, and nothing uses the network or storage.

Your code is in `index.html`, `main.js`, the modules in `src/` and `README.md`; `three` is the only npm dependency.

**Housekeeping:** I previewed with esbuild's in-memory server and kept screenshots in a scratch `.preview/` folder, which I've deleted, so no build output is left behind. When stopping the preview server I killed every process matching `tail -f /dev/null`, which would also have caught any unrelated process of yours with that command line. I didn't touch the Python server already running on port 8123.
